Q: How to run a preinstall-like script in Yarn Berry? A:

In Yarn Berry (Yarn 2+), the way to run lifecycle scripts like preinstall has changed compared to Yarn Classic (v1).

Key points:

  • Yarn Berry does not support preinstall and postinstall scripts directly in the same way as Yarn Classic.

  • Instead, Yarn Berry encourages using packageExtensions or hooks in .yarnrc.yml for advanced workflows.

  • For running scripts before install, you typically use the prepare or preinstall hooks in your package's package.json but with some caveats.

How to run a preinstall-like script in Yarn Berry

  1. Use scripts.preinstall in package.json
    Yarn Berry supports lifecycle scripts like preinstall but with some differences. It runs preinstall scripts inside the package itself after dependencies are resolved but before the package is installed.

    Example in package.json:

    {
  "scripts": {
    "preinstall": "echo Running preinstall script"
  }
}

    This works if you run yarn install in that package.

  2. If you want a global preinstall hook (before any install), use Yarn hooks

    Yarn Berry supports hooks via .yarnrc.yml:

    hooks:
  beforeAllInstalled: "./scripts/preinstall.sh"

    This runs a script before Yarn installs any packages.

  3. Use prepare script if your goal is to run build steps before publishing or installing a package

    The prepare script runs before the package is packed and published, and also runs after installation if the package is a git dependency.

  4. Workarounds for complex preinstall logic

    If you want to run a script before any install in a monorepo or project, you could:

    • Use a custom script that runs your preinstall logic, then calls yarn install.

    • Use Yarn plugins or hooks as above.

Q: How to generate QR Code on PDF file in flutter A:

Set drawText to false :

pw.BarcodeWidget(
  data: 'my-qr-content',
  width: 40,
  height: 40,

Q: ciscoconfparse in Python 3.4 module doesn't import correctly A:

Is there any reason the install may not be working? Or else what is the best way to include the module with my own project?

ciscoconfparse version 1.1.1 failed in all Python3 versions due to broken relative imports.

Relative imports broke due to lack of compliance with PEP 366 in ciscoconfparse version 1.1.1 (and prior); to resolve this, ciscoconfparse added a __main__.py in the package. I manually tested this against Python2.7 and Python3.4.1; as far as I can tell, version 1.1.2 fixes the issues with Python3.

FYI, ciscoconfparse is deprecated; please use ciscoconfparse2. Full-disclosure, I am the author.

Q: ciscoconfparse unable to import python3.7 win10 A:

I have reproduced the bug where Win10 and Python 3.7.0 cause problems.

FWIW, if you completely uninstall Python 3.7.0 (including manually deleting your Windows installation directory tree), then install Python 3.7.1, you should not have this problem with Windows 10.

BTW, ciscoconfparse is deprecated; please use ciscoconfparse2. Full-disclosure, I am the author.

Q: How to generate a matrix with every offset of vector without using a for loop A:

You can try

> v <- c(1, 3, 7, 2, 5)

> m <- matrix(NA, 2 * length(v) - 1, length(v))

> `[<-`(m, (row(m) + col(m)) %in% (seq_along(v) + length(v)), v)
      [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4] [,5]
 [1,]   NA   NA   NA   NA    1
 [2,]   NA   NA   NA    1    3
 [3,]   NA   NA    1    3    7
 [4,]   NA    1    3    7    2
 [5,]    1    3    7    2    5
 [6,]    3    7    2    5   NA
 [7,]    7    2    5   NA   NA
 [8,]    2    5   NA   NA   NA
 [9,]    5   NA   NA   NA   NA

Q: What is the difference between 'Map.entry(k, v)' and 'AbstractMap.SimpleImmutableEntry::new'? A:

As mentioned by @VGR in a comment, you should look at the Javadoc of Map::entry(K,V) and AbstractMap.SimpleImmutableEntry to see their objective differences.

Since (Year) Extendable Allow null Serializable Value-based
Map::entry(K,V) Java 9 (2017) ❌No ❌No ❌No ✅Yes
SimpleImmutableEntry Java 6 (2006) ✅Yes ✅Yes ✅Yes ❌No

And it should be noted that the former is a static factory method, whereas the latter is a class that you instantiate directly via a constructor.

At a more subjective level, the Map::entry(K,V) method is the better designed API for when you simply want an unmodifiable Map.Entry.

  • It's scoped to the Map interface instead of a relatively arbitrary abstract implementation. That makes it more convenient, which was the primary goal of JEP 269: Convenience Factory Methods for Collections, and arguably more readable.
  • The implementation is not public API. That makes it easier to change the implementation as the language evolves.
  • User code can't extend Map::entry(K,V), unlike the non-final SimpleImmutableEntry class. That means there's a stronger guarantee the implementation does not break the contract.

You should prefer Map::entry(K,V) over SimpleImmutableEntry unless you really need to allow null keys or values, or really need the entry to be serializable.

That all said, the primary purpose of Map::entry(K,V) is for creating an unmodifiable Map from entries. For example:

import static java.util.Map.entry;
import java.util.Map;

class Example {

  static final Map<String, String> MAP = 
      Map.ofEntries(
          entry("key1", "value1"),
          entry("key2", "value2"),
          entry("key3", "value3"),
          entry("key4", "value4"),
          entry("key5", "value5"));
}

And the primary purpose of AbstractMap.Simple[Immutable]Entry is to aid in creating your own Map implementation, particularly one that inherits from AbstractMap.

If you need a tuple outside the context of a Map then consider creating a record specific to your domain. At the least, your domain-specific type will have more appropriate naming than the general "Entry", "key", and "value" names. For example, having:

record Point(int x, int y) {}

Would be better than using Map.Entry<Integer, Integer>.

Q: Create stored procedures from create and select statements A:

If you absolutely had to store this information in a table, it sounds like it would only be needed temporarily as part of the process of fixing the data.

Rather than creating a table each time you run the code and then dropping it after you're done with it (which is what I assume your plan is for this table!), why not create a Global Temporary Table (GTT) once, and then use that to store data on a per session basis - ie. only your session can see the data that's been stored there during that session.

Q: Java multithreading and SWING A:

What you want to do is the standard way most designers would want to do it, that is, have a background worker class which is independent of the GUI.

Creating a class, MySwingWorker, which extends SwingWorker and which calls your background classes is the standard approach. You may want to create one or more dialog classes to wrap your usage of MySwingWorkers, depending on the complexity of your application.
